Tiria
TIR-ee-ah
n. (a son of Jehaleleel of the tribe of Judah, named once)
Hebrew Tirya, fear, or reverence; taken by some from yare', to fear; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:16.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tiria is the third of the four sons of Jehaleleel in the genealogy of Judah: “And the sons of Jehaleleel; Ziph, and Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel” (1 Chronicles 4:16). The verse stands in the long Judahite register that the Chronicler assembled after the captivity, when a returned remnant needed to know whose land was whose and which families had a claim in the tribe of the promise. Tiria is a name in that proof of title and nothing more; no act, no dwelling, no son is recorded of him. The chapter around him is full of such men, and a few of them get a sentence of narrative — Jabez his prayer, Caleb his inheritance — while the rest stand in the column. The Chronicler's purpose governs the whole: Judah was the tribe of the sceptre, and the line had to be shown unbroken from Judah to David and past David to the men then living. Tiria belongs to that demonstration. Scripture troubles itself to preserve the name of a man of whom nothing else survives, because the tribe he stood in was the tribe out of which Christ came: “For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda” (Hebrews 7:14).

He is the third of the four sons of Jehaleleel.

Key Scripture

1Ch 4:16 — "And the sons of Jehaleleel; Ziph, and Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel."

1Ch 4:1 — "The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal."

Heb 7:14 — "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood."

Gen 49:10 — "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be."

Modern Corruption

The Chronicler's registers are read as priestly invention; they are a returned remnant's documentation of title in the tribe from which Christ came.

expand to see more

Critical treatment of 1 and 2 Chronicles has long cast the genealogies as a post-exilic construction serving the interests of the temple establishment. The books present themselves otherwise, and the use the lists are put to is plain on the face of them: a people returning to a land after seventy years needed to establish who belonged to which family and which family held which portion. The registers are legal in character. That is why they include men like Tiria of whom nothing else is said — an invented list supplies stories, and a surveyed list supplies names.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the genealogies of Judah are Christological before they are tribal. Jacob's blessing had fixed the sceptre in Judah, and the Chronicler is tracing the tribe that would produce the King. Every obscure name in 1 Chronicles 4 is part of the kept record of the line, and the keeping of it was the LORD's work through men who thought they were only counting households.
